units: a neighbourhood has two distinct ways of putting a request to a local authority
the first route rests on a document taken round for people to sign
this route calls for very little in the way of materials
the authority is obliged to keep the written request
a signed document shows neither the disagreements nor the shades of opinion
the second route means gathering people in a hall open to all
the meeting lets opposing views answer one another directly
those who cannot get out of the house are shut out of the meeting
background noise puts the quieter speakers at a disadvantage
the two routes complete each other, one measuring the discontent and the other explaining it
text: When a neighbourhood wants a local authority to consider a request, it has two quite different routes available. The first is a written request carried round from door to door for signature. It costs almost nothing, it can be prepared in a single evening, and it leaves behind a record the authority is obliged to keep. Its weakness is silence: a signed sheet reveals none of the shading, and nobody argues an objection out on paper. The second route is a meeting in a hall thrown open to anyone who cares to attend. There, opposing views answer one another immediately. But whoever cannot get out of the house is excluded altogether, and the general din drowns the quieter speakers. Neither route replaces the other. The signed sheet measures how much discontent exists; the meeting explains what lies behind it.

units: a repair van came regularly to set up on the square of a very modest village
the children arrived first, drawn by the noise and the smell of the workshop
people brought damaged things, among them a seat and a faulty lamp
a woman insisted on keeping a coffee grinder despite the state of it
every owner told how their thing had come to break
the craftsman listened without turning his eyes from his cutting bench
the square emptied little by little while the craftsman packed his crates
the narrator sees in these visits the proof that nothing was thrown out without an argument
text: Every week the repair van pulled up at the edge of the square, and the whole of that small hamlet seemed to open at once. The children came first, drawn by the smell of hot metal and by the racket of the grinder. Then came the objects: a chair whose seat had given way, a lamp with a bared wire, a coffee grinder that its owner would not be parted from. Then came the stories, for nobody went home without saying how the crack had happened in the first place. The mender listened without ever lifting his eyes from the bench, nodding in the right places. When he shut his crates the square emptied slowly, the way a hall empties after a concert. What he carried off with him was not only scrap metal. It was proof, renewed every week, that nothing here was thrown out before someone had spoken up for it.

units: preparation starts with a list of the water points and the power points available
a notice goes up by the entrance a week before the operation
this notice gives the time, the expected length and the equipment to bring
who does what is set down in writing the day before
you must check that the road running along the building is clear of bins
cleaning starts with the high parts before working down towards the ground
starting at the bottom would mean doing part of the cleaning twice
the equipment is put away before the last break, while the volunteers are still there
a written note of the damage goes to the manager at the end
text: Before you organise a clean-up in a shared yard, list the taps and the power points that you can actually make use of. A week ahead, put a notice up by the entrance giving the time, how long the work is expected to take and what equipment people should bring with them. The day before, set out who does what in writing, because a spoken instruction goes straight out of the head. On the morning itself, gather the volunteers by the gate and check that the road running along the building is clear of bins. Start high, with the gutters and the ledges, then work down towards the ground; the other way round means doing half of it twice over. Put the equipment away before the last break, while the volunteers are all still together. Finish with a written note of the damage, handed to the building manager.

units: a retaining wall collapsed in an old part of town
the collapse led to the closing of the road serving the foot of the slope
with no alternative route, traffic shifted into a narrow lane
buses cannot pass each other in that lane
people living nearby report repeated delays
a crowd formed outside a room far too small when a meeting was announced
the technical services put the damage down to an old seepage made worse by rain
the repair will take several weeks because the ground has to be surveyed first
a temporary walkway has shortened the detours without removing the congestion
text: A retaining wall gave way at the weekend in an old part of town, and the road serving the foot of the slope was shut off at once. With no alternative route on offer, the traffic shifted into a narrow lane where two buses cannot pass each other. Residents describe delays that build on one another, and a crush at the single stop still in use. When a public meeting was announced, a crowd formed outside a community room far too small to hold everyone who had come along to it. The technical services put the collapse down to a long-standing seepage, made a good deal worse by weeks of steady rain. Repairs will take several weeks, since the ground has to be surveyed before a fresh footing can be poured. A temporary walkway has been laid, which has shortened the detours without easing the congestion.

units: the reception hall sits on the lower floor of a low building
the light comes from a grimy skylight
a single counter works behind a glass panel with an opening cut into it
the queue stretches as far as the entrance door
people coming and going in search of a form break the queue
the waiting sets off arguments about whose turn it is
coloured tokens are now handed out on arrival
a board shows the colour being called and seats have been put in
the counter works at the same rate but the quarrels have almost stopped
text: The reception hall takes up the lower floor of a squat building, lit from above by a skylight thick with grime. A single counter works there, behind a glass panel with a round opening cut into it. In front of it the queue stretches all the way to the door, broken again and again by people wandering off in search of a form. Waiting breeds friction: places are disputed out loud, and newcomers are accused of pushing in. Since last season the desk has handed out wooden tokens marked with a colour as people arrive. A board shows which colour is being called, and benches have been set out along the wall. People sit down, watch the board, and stop watching each other. The counter works at the rate it always did, yet the quarrels have all but gone from a hall that used to be a loud one.

units: the writer disputes the idea that help between neighbours has gone
in the block of his childhood, tools were borrowed from the door opposite
an elderly resident minded the children without being asked
where he lives now, people pass on the stairs without speaking
that same block produced volunteers to repaint a bike store
a list of people willing to put the bins out was drawn up there
the writer puts the change down to the channel used and not to selfishness
help now goes through written messages and a notice board
the writer prefers reserved but reliable neighbours to nosy ones
text: People keep telling me that neighbours no longer help one another, and I say it has only changed its shape. In the block where I grew up, you knocked on the door opposite whenever you needed to borrow a spanner, and the lady on the top floor minded the children without ever being asked. Where I live now, nothing of the sort: we pass one another on the stairs without a word. So what? That same staircase produced two volunteers last season to repaint the bike store, and a list of residents willing to put the bins out. The difference is not selfishness, it is the channel. Helping used to require closeness; nowadays it goes through a written message and a board by the letter boxes. Give me quiet neighbours who turn up when it matters over talkative ones who sit in judgement.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)

she turns down the chair that is regularly offered to her
a member reckons that without her the till and the plans would be empty
text: Her office fits inside a cupboard, and once a week she pulls out of it a folder as thick as a brick. As treasurer of a neighbourhood association, she takes in the subscriptions, chases the ones who forget, and writes every sum down by hand before copying it into a spreadsheet. She also bargains: the loan of a hall next door, a discount from a printer, a bill put off, the patience of a disgruntled landlord. And she rules on spending, because the demands compete for one small till: cloth for the sewing group, a repair to the copier, refreshments for the open meetings. Each time the committee is renewed she turns down the chair, saying that accounts kept properly weigh more than any title. Without her, says a member stacking chairs, the till would be empty and so would the plans.

units: the opening of the performance looked unpromising
the stage held nothing but a bare floor and mismatched seats
the amateur players seemed tense
the first scene suffered from a script too carefully written and poorly inhabited
the room went quiet when an actress picked up a dropped bunch of keys without breaking her line
the show gained in pace from that mishap onwards
short scenes followed one another and the thin set stopped mattering
the closing sequence ran without a word and showed neighbours ignoring each other
the reviewer judges that the script must be shortened
the reviewer reckons the company would deserve a bigger hall
text: Nothing at the start of the performance promised what followed: a bare stage, three mismatched chairs, amateur players visibly stiff with nerves. The opening scene suffered from a script too carefully written, recited by voices rather than carried by them. Then the room fell quiet of its own accord when an actress playing a caretaker dropped her bunch of keys and picked it up without breaking off her line. From there the evening found its pace. Short scenes followed one another, the weariness of some answering the stubbornness of others, and the thin set stopped mattering. The closing sequence, played without a word, seemed to me the truest of all: neighbours passing on a staircase without recognising each other. The script wants tightening. The company deserves a bigger hall.

the return of the pressure will bring a noisy purge that is harmless
a whistling water heater must be reported to the manager
the cost will be covered by the shared payment already made
text: Dear neighbours, the water will be off in both staircases tomorrow afternoon. The cause is a corroded stopcock in the basement whose handle will no longer turn. Since that one fitting controls the whole rising main, nothing can be done on the upper floors until it has been replaced. The corrosion comes from a slow leak that took a long while to find, because it ran straight into a drain grating. In practice: fill two containers per household the evening before, and close your own taps while the supply is off, so that nothing floods when the pressure returns. The plumber expects a noisy purge on restart, as trapped air will set the pipes shaking, which is harmless. If your water heater whistles afterwards, report it without delay. The cost is covered by the shared payment already made.

units: the question raised concerns a rise in the members' yearly payment
the present takings no longer cover the upkeep of the premises
the treasurer thinks the rise modest but fears shutting out the poorer members
the committee suggests opening the premises to outside users for a payment
the quiet spells are what this opening is aimed at
premises left empty cost as much as premises in use
the bookings would be handled by members taking turns
a single register would prevent promises that contradict each other
a review would be discussed at a general meeting if the takings still fell short
the course chosen pairs a limited rise with partial hiring
text: Should the yearly subscription go up? The question arises because the takings no longer cover the upkeep of the premises. The treasurer answers that the rise would be a modest one, yet it would shut out the members with least to spare. Is there another way? Yes, says the committee: let outside users hire the premises during the quiet spells. An empty hall costs no less to keep than a busy one. Who would handle the bookings? A desk staffed by members in turn, working from a single register so that nothing is promised twice over. And if the money still fell short? The committee undertakes to reopen the matter at a general meeting rather than settle it alone. The course chosen pairs a limited rise with partial hiring, so the effort is shared out instead of falling on a few.
